Shortly after, he converted his 1998 Volkswagen Jetta and affixed a bumper sticker reading, *"This vehicle runs on straight vegetable oil."* 

"For a single bumper sticker, I was surprised at how many people stopped me and said, 'Hey, how do you do that?'" Winston recalls.

Prior to his first conversion, Winston had not worked on an automobile since driving his 1978 Plymouth Volare in college. Today, he estimates that fewer than 10,000 converted diesel vehicles are currently on the road nationwide. Turning his hobby into a business, he now sells and installs conversion kits, making him the only provider offering this specialized service in the Washington, D.C. area. 

Although his side venture, FeedMyWheels.com, has converted only a handful of automobiles to date, he recently embarked on his most ambitious undertaking yet: a 1983 Itasca RV.

"There's a lot of trial and error," Winston acknowledges. 

Over a demanding two-day process, he encountered numerous setbacks, including repeatedly drained batteries and alternator troubles. By the end of the second day, as Winston prepared to fill the RV's 40-gallon tank with recycled grease from a local Chinese restaurant, a neighboring bystander accidentally knocked over an 80-gallon holding tank. Tens of gallons of pungent, brown oil spilled onto the street. 

Unfazed, Winston quipped, "It's OK—earthworms love this stuff."

After nearly 50 hours of cutting, fitting, and reattaching hoses, Winston successfully started the RV and switched the engine over to the vegetable oil system. He notes that emissions from vegetable oil are roughly half those of standard petroleum-based diesel fuel. 

"If you're emitting half the carbon dioxide that your neighbor is, that means one of two things: Either your neighbor can drive twice as much, or you're having a significant positive impact on the environment," Winston explains. "In some small way, we're contributing to saving the environment. It's going to save a glacier somewhere."

**From Fryer to Fuel Tank: How One Accountant Brought Green Transportation to the D.C. Area**

By day, Josh Winston balances spreadsheets, navigates tax codes, and manages balance sheets. But when the workday ends, the Washington, D.C.-based accountant trades his calculator for a set of wrenches and steps into a world powered by grease. Driven by a desire to find practical, low-cost alternatives to traditional fossil fuels, Winston launched a side business dedicated to converting standard diesel vehicles to run on recycled vegetable oil—a waste product readily available behind local restaurants and diners.

The technology behind vegetable oil conversions relies on a clever workaround to a simple mechanical problem. While conventional diesel engines can easily burn vegetable oil, untreated oil is far thicker than diesel fuel and can clog an engine’s injectors when cold. To solve this, Winston sells and installs specialized modification kits that add a secondary fuel system. Vehicles start on standard diesel, and once the engine coolant heats up a custom heat exchanger, the system automatically switches to vegetable oil. 

The path to building a successful conversion business, however, was paved with trial, error, and grease-stained hands. Complex projects often pushed Winston’s engineering skills to their limits. His hardest test came with the modification of a bulky 1983 Recreational Vehicle. The aging motorhome presented a maze of technical setbacks: deteriorating stock plumbing, tight clearance in the engine bay, and difficulty maintaining the high oil temperatures required to move a heavy vehicle. For weeks, Winston wrestled with fuel-flow restrictions, clogged filters, and stubborn electrical shorts. Yet, through persistence and custom-fabricated routing, he successfully transformed the 1983 RV into a fully functional, vegetable-powered home on wheels.

That success proved to be a turning point. As news of his work spread through word-of-mouth and green-living forums, Winston established himself as the sole specialized provider of vegetable oil conversions in the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area. From classic Mercedes-Benz sedans to heavy-duty pickup trucks and delivery vans, he has successfully converted a wide variety of vehicles, giving them a second life as low-emission, carbon-neutral road warriors.

Winston’s journey highlights a growing public appetite for accessible, grassroots sustainability. While electric vehicles often dominate the headlines regarding green transit, his flourishing side business demonstrates that innovative, immediate solutions are already within reach. counterfactuals.output:
**BETHESDA, Maryland (CNN) —** By day, Josh Winston lives in a world of absolute precision. As a senior tax accountant at a firm in downtown Bethesda, his work revolves around rigid spreadsheets, corporate ledgers, and pristine, unwrinkled dress shirts. 

By night, however, Winston’s world smells distinctly of fast-food french fries. 

Stepping into his two-car garage—a space crammed with custom plumbing, heating coils, 55-gallon drums, and the faint lingering aroma of tempura batter—the 38-year-old trades his mechanical pencil for a torque wrench. 

Winston is the founder and sole operator of *GreaseWorks Conversions*, a boutique side business that transforms standard diesel vehicles and massive motorhomes into eco-friendly machines powered entirely by waste vegetable oil.

"An accountant's job is to look at a system, find the waste, and optimize it," Winston says, wiping a smudge of dark grease from his cheek with the back of a gloved hand. "When I look at thousands of gallons of spent fryer oil getting dumped into rendered waste bins behind local diners every week, while diesel sits at over four bucks a gallon, all I see is a massive inefficiency waiting to be solved."

### From Math to Mechanics

The idea was born four years ago during a cross-country road trip. Winston and his wife rented a heavy, diesel-guzzling RV. Watching the numbers rapidly tick up at every gas pump triggered his analytical instincts. 

"We spent almost $2,000 just on fuel," he recalls. "I came home obsessed with finding a cheaper, cleaner way to keep those big engines moving."

He spent months researching alternative fuels, eventually settling on Straight Vegetable Oil (SVO). Unlike biodiesel, which requires a complex chemical process to turn oil into a refined fuel, SVO systems allow an engine to run directly on raw, filtered cooking grease collected from restaurant waste bins.

The catch? Vegetable oil is much thicker than standard diesel fuel. If you pour cold canola oil straight into a modern engine, it will clog the fuel injectors and ruin the system. 

That is where Winston’s conversion kits come in.

He installs a specialized "two-tank" system. The vehicle starts up using its normal diesel tank. As the engine warms up, hot coolant is routed through custom heat exchangers wrapped around a second, newly installed fuel tank containing filtered vegetable oil. 

Once the oil reaches roughly 160 degrees Fahrenheit, its viscosity thins to match that of standard diesel. With the flick of a toggle switch on the dashboard, a solenoid valve swaps the fuel line from diesel to grease. Just before reaching their destination, drivers flip the switch back for a few miles to purge the fuel lines with clean diesel so the engine can start cold the next day.

### The Van-Life Boom

What started as a DIY experiment on Winston’s own 2002 Ford Excursion has blossomed into a bustling weekend enterprise. His primary clientele? Eco-conscious road-trippers, budget-savvy retirees, and digital nomads riding the post-pandemic "van-life" wave.

"Josh converted my 32-foot Class C Winnebago last spring," says Marcus Vance, a freelance photographer who travels full-time. "I just completed a 6,000-mile trip through the Southwest. I spent less than $300 on diesel total. The rest of the time, I was running on free oil I scored from seafood joints and donut shops along the way. People laugh when I tell them my exhaust smells like funnel cake, but my bank account isn't complaining."

Winston charges between $3,500 and $6,000 for a conversion, depending on the vehicle's size and complexity. For a heavy RV that gets 8 to 10 miles per gallon, he calculates that most customers break even within 12,000 miles of driving.

"It’s basic math," Winston says with a smile. "The ROI is undeniable."

### The Hunt for "Yellow Gold"

Converting the vehicle is only half the equation; finding the fuel is the other. 

Winston has built a network of partnerships with dozens of local Maryland and D.C. restaurants. Many small eateries pay rendering companies to haul away their used fryer oil. Winston offers to take it off their hands for free, rolling up on Saturday mornings with a custom trailer equipped with a high-powered pump and a multi-stage filtration system.

"Josh is a lifesaver," says Steve Kyriakos, owner of a fish and chips spot in Silver Spring. "He’s reliable, he keeps our back alley clean, and honestly, it feels good knowing our old cooking oil is driving a motorhome across the country instead of sitting in a landfill."

However, the SVO lifestyle isn't for everyone. It requires hands-on effort. Drivers must filter their own oil if they source it directly from restaurants, usually passing it through fine mesh bags down to 1 micron to remove food particles and water.

There are also legal and logistical hurdles. Fuel tax laws vary by state, and while the EPA permits SVO conversions under specific guidelines, sourcing clean oil in dense urban areas can sometimes turn into a competitive sport among "greasers."

### Balancing Act

Back in his garage, Winston steps back to admire his latest project: a slick, silver 2008 Mercedes Sprinter camper van belonging to a couple planning a trip to Alaska. 

He turns the key. The diesel engine rumbles to life. He waits a few minutes for the temperature gauge to rise, then flips a small blue toggle switch labeled "FRY." 

The engine note shifts slightly—smoothing out into a quiet, steady purr. Seconds later, a warm, savory scent drifts out of the tailpipe, reminiscent of a Sunday morning brunch spot.

Winston has no plans to quit his accounting day job. He likes the stability of his corporate career, and he insists that keeping *GreaseWorks* small allows him to focus on quality over volume. But as fuel prices fluctuate and environmental concerns grow, his weekend schedule remains booked months in advance.

"During the week, I help people balance their financial books," Winston says, flipping off the shop lights as the garage door slowly closes. "On the weekend, I help them balance their carbon footprint. Honestly? Both feel pretty rewarding."

**From french fry grease to the open road: How one man converted a 1983 RV to run on recycled cooking oil**

**EUGENE, Oregon (CNN) —** To the casual observer, Marcus Vance’s 1983 Itasca Sunflyer looks like a vintage relic of American road-trip nostalgia. Painted in classic 1980s tones of tan and muted brown, the 27-foot motorhome commands attention on the highway. 

But as it rolls past, there’s one distinct difference: it smells faintly of fresh fish and chips.

Vance, a 34-year-old carpenter and self-taught mechanic from Eugene, Oregon, recently completed a weekend transformation of the RV’s 6.2-liter Detroit Diesel engine. The rig no longer relies solely on traditional pump fuel. Instead, it runs almost entirely on waste vegetable oil (WVO) sourced directly from the deep fryers of a local diner down the street.

"People think you need a $100,000 electric vehicle to reduce your carbon footprint," Vance told CNN, leaning against the chrome bumper of his beloved motorhome. "I bought this rig for $3,000. By turning someone else's trash into my fuel, I’m traveling for free while keeping gallons of grease out of the local waste stream."

### A high-stakes, 48-hour build

Converting a conventional diesel engine to burn vegetable oil isn't as simple as pouring fryer grease straight into the tank. Because vegetable oil is far thicker than standard diesel, it must be heated to roughly 160 degrees Fahrenheit to thin its viscosity before it enters the engine's injectors. 

Vance set aside a single weekend to install a customized dual-tank system—a deadline he quickly realized was overly optimistic. 

"I thought it was going to be a smooth two-day project," Vance said with a laugh. "The RV had other plans."

**Day One: Rust and broken lines**

The project began Saturday morning with Vance attempting to tap into the engine's coolant system to power a custom heat exchanger. The plan was to use the engine's own heat to warm the oil tank mounted in the rear storage bay. 

However, four decades of wear and tear immediately stalled progress. 

"The moment I tried to back out the 40-year-old brass fittings on the fuel return line, the whole thing snapped off in the housing," Vance recalled. "It was rust-welded shut. I spent four hours on Saturday just drilling out a broken bolt and retapping the threads. By sunset on Day One, I hadn't even mounted the second fuel tank yet."

**Day Two: Electrical fires and coolant leaks**

Determined to finish by Sunday night, Vance worked under portable work lights into the early hours of the morning. But Day Two brought even steeper challenges. 

When testing the crucial three-way solenoid valve—the switch that allows the driver to toggle between standard diesel for starting the engine and vegetable oil for cruising—a short circuit caused a spark. 

"I saw a plume of white smoke come out from under the dashboard," Vance said. "A wire harness had melted. For about ten minutes, I thought I’d completely ruined the RV's electrical system."

After splicing in new wiring and adding an inline fuse, Vance faced his final hurdle: a high-pressure coolant leak from the heat exchanger that soaked his driveway in bright green antifreeze just two hours before his Sunday evening deadline. 

Undeterred, Vance replaced the crushed rubber gaskets with heavy-duty silicone seals, bled the air from the lines, and finally turned the key at 11:30 p.m. Sunday night. The engine sputtered, caught, and hummed smoothly as the valve switched over to recycled oil.

### Powered by the local diner

The lifeblood of Vance’s road trips comes courtesy of *The Daily Fry*, a family-owned diner located just three miles from his home. 

Owner Sarah Lin used to pay a commercial disposal company to haul away the dozens of gallons of spent canola oil generated by her kitchen every week. Now, she simply sets it aside for Vance, who filters it through a 5-micron mesh bag in his garage before pumping it into the Itasca.

"It’s a win-win," Lin told CNN. "Marcus gets to go on his adventures, we save on waste removal fees, and we get a kick out of knowing our fry oil is powering a road trip across the Pacific Northwest."

### Old tech, modern sustainability

While electric motorhomes remain prohibitively expensive and rare on the market, Vance believes retrofitting older diesel vehicles offers an accessible path forward for middle-class DIYers interested in sustainability. 

The total cost of Vance's conversion kit, including hoses, valves, and the secondary tank, came out to just under $900—an investment he estimates will pay for itself in fuel savings within his first two long-distance trips.

"There’s something poetic about taking a heavy, gas-guzzling icon of 1980s consumer culture and turning it into a zero-net-carbon machine," Vance said. "It took a lot of scraped knuckles, a few gray hairs, and two very long days, but standing here watching it run on grease? I’d do it all over again."

Vance plans to test the Itasca's new system on a 1,200-mile maiden voyage along the Oregon coast next month—with a trunk full of filtered cooking oil and a map of local diners along the route.

**WASHINGTON —** If you get stuck behind Arthur Pendelton’s 1984 Mercedes-Benz 300D in bumper-to-bumper traffic on the Capital Beltway, your nose might trick you. Amid the sea of carbon monoxide and standard exhaust, Pendelton’s tailpipe leaves behind a distinctly savory aroma: fresh French fries.

By day, Pendelton is a mild-mannered senior auditor at a K Street accounting firm, dressed in crisp oxfords and immersed in tax codes. But step into his two-car garage in Silver Spring, Maryland, on a Saturday morning, and the spreadsheet-cruncher vanishes. In his place stands a grease-stained DIY mechanic, surrounded by 55-gallon drums, copper heating coils, and filtration pumps. 

Pendelton, 42, is the founder and sole operator of *Feed My Wheels*, a boutique service that converts conventional diesel vehicles to run on straight waste vegetable oil (WVO)—the very grease local restaurants pay to throw away.

“In accounting, everything has to balance. You’re looking for efficiency, looking to eliminate waste,” Pendelton says, wiping a smudge of black engine oil off his forehead with the back of his forearm. “Converting a diesel engine is the ultimate balancing act. You take a waste product that’s bound for a landfill and turn it into zero-net-carbon fuel. The math just makes sense.”

Pendelton started *Feed My Wheels* four years ago as a personal weekend project. Frustrated by the high cost of living in the D.C. metro area and driven by a desire to lower his environmental footprint, he bought a rusty conversion kit online and modified his own car. Soon, friends were asking for help. Then friends of friends. Today, *Feed My Wheels* has a three-month waiting list, serving an eclectic mix of clients—from suburban dads and eco-conscious college professors to D.C. policy wonks looking to practice what they preach.

The technology behind the conversion isn't new; in fact, Rudolf Diesel designed his original engine in 1893 to run on peanut oil. But Pendelton’s kits modernize the process for daily commuters. 

He installs a secondary fuel tank in the vehicle’s trunk or truck bed, complete with glowing heated fuel lines routed from the engine’s coolant system. Because thick vegetable oil must be warmed to roughly 160 degrees Fahrenheit to flow easily through fuel injectors, the car starts up on standard diesel. Once the engine reaches temperature, a flick of a toggle switch on the dashboard reroutes the fuel line to the veggie tank. Just before turning the car off, the driver flips the switch back to purge the lines with diesel for the next cold start.

“It takes a little bit of discipline,” Pendelton admits. “You can’t just turn the key and forget about it like a modern electric vehicle. You have to pay attention to your machine. But for the people who come to me, that’s part of the romance.”

Sourcing the fuel is half the adventure. Pendelton has built a network of handshakes with local D.C.-area eateries—from a Thai restaurant in Adams Morgan to an old-school diner in Arlington. Every week, he picks up spent oil from their fryers, takes it home, and runs it through a multi-stage gravity filtration system in his backyard shed. 

For his customers, the financial and environmental payoff is sweet. With average D.C.-area gas prices remaining unpredictable, *Feed My Wheels* clients are driving for pennies on the gallon—the only real cost being the time it takes to filter their own grease.

“Arthur changed the way I think about energy,” says Sarah Jenkins, a high school biology teacher from Bethesda who had her 2003 Volkswagen Jetta TDI converted by *Feed My Wheels* last year. “My commute used to cost me $200 a month. Now, it costs me a couple of hours on a Sunday filtering oil I got for free from a local egg roll shop. And my students think I drive a magic car.”

Despite the growing popularity of commercial electric vehicles, Pendelton believes there will always be a place for the scrappy, decentralized ethos of the vegetable oil community. EVs are great, he says, but they rely on an electric grid that still largely burns fossil fuels.

“Veggie oil is true recycling,” Pendelton says, leaning over the engine bay of a customer’s Ford F-250, double-checking a fuel valve connection. “It’s hyper-local, it’s low-tech, and it builds community. You end up making friends with the guy who owns the donut shop down the street because he’s fueling your drive to work.”

As the sun sets over Silver Spring, Pendelton packs up his tools, washes his hands with heavy-duty orange soap, and prepares to step back into the world of balance sheets and tax returns. But before he heads inside, he fires up his old Mercedes. The engine turns over with a comforting, mechanical purr, sending a faint whiff of hot canola oil into the cool evening air. 

He smiles, flips the dashboard switch, and prepares to feed his wheels.

**BETHESDA DAILY NEWS**

**From Fryer to Freeway: Bethesda Mechanic Transforms Cars to Run on Veggie Oil**

**By Local News Desk**  
**BETHESDA, Md. —** If you walk down Norfolk Avenue on a Tuesday afternoon, you might catch a sudden, overpowering craving for French fries. But the scent isn’t coming from a local bistro—it’s drifting out of the tailpipe of a 2002 Ford F-250, newly retrofitted by local mechanic and environmental enthusiast Josh Winston.

Winston is the founder of *Feed My Wheels*, a Bethesda-based boutique shop specializing in converting standard diesel vehicles to run on recycled waste vegetable oil (WVO). Over the past three years, Winston has turned a passion for sustainable engineering into a booming local business, sourcing spent cooking oil from Montgomery County restaurants and giving it a second life on the Beltway.

"Most people look at a vat of dirty grease behind a restaurant and see trash," Winston said, leaning over the engine bay of a Mercedes-Benz wagon. "I look at it and see carbon-neutral fuel."

The conversion process involves installing a secondary fuel tank, heated fuel lines—necessary to thin the thick oil before it reaches the engine—and an automated switching system. Vehicles start up on traditional diesel and, once the engine reaches optimal temperature, automatically switch over to vegetable oil. 

For Winston, the initiative is about much more than just saving money at the pump; it's a direct response to global climate change. 

"Every gallon of waste oil we burn instead of petroleum is a tiny, tangible victory for the planet," Winston said while adjusting a custom fuel injector. "People think individual action doesn't matter, but if we actually want to save the glaciers, we have to start swapping out fossil fuels right here in our own driveways. We can't wait for someone else to fix it."

However, turning kitchen grease into commute fuel isn't without its slippery setbacks. 

Just last week, *Feed My Wheels* hit a literal bump in the road. While Winston was transport-testing a newly modified station wagon loaded with 30 gallons of filtered canola oil, a faulty seal on an auxiliary tank ruptured. The breakdown resulted in a slick, 15-gallon spill directly onto the pavement at the intersection of Old Georgetown Road and Woodmont Avenue.

Traffic was delayed for nearly an hour as Montgomery County Hazmat and emergency crews rushed to spread bags of absorbent clay over the golden puddle to prevent it from reaching local storm drains. 

"It was an absolute nightmare, and honestly, the whole intersection smelled like a county fair food truck for three days," Winston admitted with a sheepish laugh. "The police officers were very professional, though one of them did ask if I had any French fries to go with the mess. We’ve since completely redesigned our transport valves to make sure it never happens again."

Despite the greasy catastrophe, Bethesda residents don't seem deterred. Winston says *Feed My Wheels* currently has a three-month waiting list for conversions. As fuel prices fluctuate and environmental concerns grow, more locals are eager to trade the gas station for the grease trap. 

For Winston, the mission remains as clear as refined canola. 

"The spill was a bad day at the office," Winston said. "But driving past a gas station knowing your car is running on leftover egg roll oil? That makes it all worth it."

**ASHEVILLE, North Carolina (CNN) —** Tailgating a 1983 Mercedes-Benz 300D up a steep, winding stretch of the Blue Ridge Parkway usually comes with an unpleasant side effect: a thick cloud of acrid diesel exhaust. 

But behind Marcus Vance’s dark-green vintage sedan, the air smells unexpectedly comforting. It smells like fresh, hot french fries.

"That's the smell of 80 cents a gallon," Vance says with a grin, tapping the fuel gauge on his dashboard. "And zero guilt."

Vance, 44, is a former industrial machinist who has spent the last eight years operating Blue Ridge Bio-Conversions out of a cinderblock garage in Asheville’s River Arts District. To his growing network of customers—ranging from budget-conscious commuters to eco-minded organic farmers—he is simply known as "The Grease Guy."

Vance specializes in a specific form of mechanical alchemy: converting conventional diesel vehicles to run on Straight Vegetable Oil (SVO), harvested directly from the grease traps and deep fryers of local restaurants. 

---

> **[WATCH: Step inside the workshop where discarded restaurant grease becomes highway fuel (3:42)]**

---

### From Sewer Threat to Tank Filler

The problem Vance is tackling is two-fold. First, conventional fossil fuels remain a primary driver of carbon emissions and volatile household budgets. Second, commercial kitchens generate millions of gallons of waste cooking oil annually—a sticky byproduct that, if improperly disposed of, clogs municipal sewer systems and creates costly "fatbergs."

"Restaurants used to have to pay waste management companies to haul this stuff away," Vance explains, standing beside a 275-gallon tote filled with viscous, amber liquid in his shop. "Now, we collect it for free, filter it down to two microns, and put it right into a vehicle tank. It’s localized energy in its purest form."

Unlike commercial biodiesel, which requires a complex chemical process using methanol and lye to strip glycerine from fat, Vance’s SVO systems heat raw vegetable oil directly on board the vehicle to match the viscosity of standard diesel.

The conversion requires a dual-tank system. Drivers start their cars on standard diesel. As the engine warms up, hot coolant is routed through a specialized heat exchanger wrapped around the secondary grease tank and fuel lines. Once the vegetable oil reaches roughly 160 degrees Fahrenheit—making it thin enough to atomize in the engine’s injectors—a valve flips automatically, switching the fuel source. Before turning the car off, the system purges itself, flushing diesel back into the lines so the engine can start cold the next morning.

The result is a closed-loop fuel system that Vance estimates cuts a vehicle’s net carbon footprint by up to 80% compared to standard petroleum diesel.

---

> **[WATCH: "It smells like egg rolls": Local drivers react to behind-the-wheel grease power (2:15)]**

---

### The "Sweet Spot" Vehicles

Not every car on the road can run on deep-fryer waste. Modern diesel engines utilize high-pressure "common rail" injection systems that are too delicate for the higher viscosity of vegetable oil. 

Vance’s sweet spot lies in older, mechanically injected diesels built between the late 1970s and mid-2000s—particularly older Volvos, Ford Powerstrokes, and legendary Mercedes-Benz engines known for their bulletproof durability.

"Marcus saved my farm's delivery van," says Sarah Jenkins, who runs a farm-to-table produce operation in neighboring Buncombe County. She had Vance convert her 2002 Ford F-250 three years ago. "We pick up waste oil from three local diners where we sell our vegetables. We deliver carrots and lettuce, pick up their old canola oil, filter it at the farm, and use it to bring next week's harvest back to market. It's a complete cycle."

Jenkins estimates the conversion, which cost her $2,200 upfront, paid for itself within seven months of driving.

---

> **[WATCH: Can your car run on fry oil? Marcus Vance breaks down the ideal engines (1:58)]**

---

### Challenges on the Horizon

Despite the obvious benefits, Vance is quick to admit that grease power isn't a silver bullet for the global climate crisis. 

The primary barrier is scale. There simply isn't enough waste cooking oil in the world to fuel the entire transportation sector. Furthermore, the supply of older, mechanically simple diesel cars is shrinking every year. 

There are also physical demands placed on the driver. Running on grease requires hands-on maintenance: drivers must routinely clean their own home filtration setups and monitor their engine temperature gauges closely.

"It’s not for someone who just wants to turn a key and never think about how their car works," Vance says, wiping grease from his hands with a rag. "It requires a shift in mindset. You become part of your own energy supply chain."

Legal and tax hurdles also exist in some states, where road usage taxes are traditionally wrapped into the price of fuel at the pump. Drivers using alternative fuels are technically required to report and pay these taxes independently, a grey area that deters some potential adopters.

### A Local Solution for a Global Problem

Still, for the community Vance has built in western North Carolina, the impact is undeniable. Blue Ridge Bio-Conversions has converted over 180 vehicles to date, diverting an estimated 50,000 gallons of waste grease from local waterways and sewers each year.

As fuel prices fluctuate and climate concerns mount, Vance sees his work not as a retro relic of 1970s DIY culture, but as a practical blueprint for community resilience.

"We spend so much time waiting for massive technological breakthroughs or government mandates to solve our environmental problems," Vance says, gesturing to an old Mercedes sitting on his hydraulic lift. "Sometimes, the solution is already sitting in a rusty barrel behind the local doughnut shop. You just need a wrench and a little imagination."
